Line Through Grid

GeometryNumber TheoryCounting
Game: A rectangle sits on a square grid with a line from one corner to the opposite corner, and the squares the line passes through are shaded; there is nothing to win.
How to play: Change the two numbers or drag the green and blue dots to resize the rectangle, and watch how many squares become shaded. The buttons show the small rectangles from the story.
Look for the math

Count the shaded squares in a few small rectangles and a pattern appears — but some rectangles have fewer than their neighbours. The reason is that the diagonal sometimes passes exactly through a corner where grid lines meet.

One new square per line crossed

Start in the top-left square: that is one. Each time the diagonal leaves a square it crosses an internal grid line, and that moves it into exactly one new square. In an M × N rectangle there are M − 1 internal horizontal lines and N − 1 internal vertical lines, all crossed once. So, as long as no two are crossed at the same moment,

S = 1 + (M − 1) + (N − 1) = M + N − 1.

This is the page's first formula. The logic test checked it for every pair of sizes up to 50, and it holds exactly when the diagonal misses the interior grid points — that is, when M and N share no factor, so their greatest common divisor is 1.

When the diagonal hits a corner

If g = gcd(M, N) is greater than 1, the diagonal goes through g − 1 interior grid points, equally spaced along the way. At each one it crosses a vertical and a horizontal line together, so it enters just one new square instead of two: one count is lost per point. The page's general formula is therefore

S = (M + N − 1) − (g − 1) = M + N − gcd(M, N).

Brute-force cell counting confirmed this for all 2,500 rectangles with M, N from 1 to 50, including the exceptional cases 2 × 4, 3 × 6 and 4 × 6. The page also remarks that the first formula is the more general one when grid lines are not evenly spaced; the second needs equal spacing to talk about gcd.

What the old applet actually paints

The Java applet decides whether to shade a cell by testing a tiny shrunken segment against the diagonal and by rejecting a cell when a corner lies within 0.1 pixels of the line. At the applet's usual canvas size (about 500 × 450) its grid cells are several pixels wide, and this matches the formula above. On a canvas smaller than a couple of pixels per cell, the guard can split a crossed cell, so the painted count can differ by one or two. This port keeps the exact formula for the shaded cells and uses the applet's own guard only in the checked transcription, not in the picture.

Try 2 × 4 and then 2 × 5: one extra column adds two squares, but one extra row that lands on a grid point adds only one.
